deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. It is the continuation of German-language lecture notes or a fair copy on ancient Greek history ('Dritter Abschnitt der Geschichte. Griechische Staaten', from the previous page), in the style of Göttingen history lectures of the period (e.g. Heeren's or a Gymnasium course).

Content, paraphrased:
(1) The Greek legend tells of two peoples who probably migrated from Asia: the Pelasgians and the Hellenes.
(2) The Pelasgians settled first in the Peloponnese. The Hellenes settled further north, around Parnassus, in the region that became Phocis.
(3) The earliest figure named among the Pelasgians is Inachus, said to have lived c. 1800 BC as a contemporary of Abraham.
(4) At first the Pelasgians lived as very rough barbarians in the most mountainous regions, in woods and caves, living on roots and acorns. They then founded Argos and Sicyon in the Peloponnese and spread to Attica.
(5) One of their kings was Ogyges, under whom a great flood is said to have occurred.
(6) From Attica they spread over Thessaly under the leaders Achaeus, Phthius and Pelasgus. There they became more civilised by taking up agriculture, and are said to have lived peacefully there from c. 1700 to 1550 BC.

The next page continues with Deucalion (c. 1550), the flood, and the genealogy Hellen → Dorus, Xuthus, Aeolus.

There are no derivations, formulas or computations to reconstruct. Red-ink corrections, probably by a second hand such as a teacher, fix spellings like 'Pelasgier' and 'Phocis'. The hand and content suggest school or student notes bound with Gauss material, not Gauss's own mathematical work.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics on the page.

Historically, the dates (Inachus c. 1800 BC, the Pelasgians in Thessaly 1700–1550 BC) are the conventional legendary chronology of late-18th/early-19th-century textbooks. They are not modern historical fact.
The pairing of Inachus with Abraham is a traditional synchronism from Eusebius-style chronography.

Line 2: 'Pelas{+g+}[-?-]ier' is the corrected 'Pelasgier'. A red-ink 'g' is inserted above.

Line 6: 'ist zu erst die Rede[?] unter Inachus [-?-]' is uncertain. The image shows roughly 'ist zu erst nach die Urd... Inachus' with a red correction and a struck word before 'c. 1800'. 'Inachus' is plausible.

Line 12: the leader names 'Achäus, Phthius und Pelasgus' fit the image and the mythological tradition (sons of Larissa). 'Thessalien' carries a red-ink correction, and 'Pelasgus' has a red superscript insertion.
